match.reason: Neither bank point teaches frequency tables or segmented bar charts; mat-displaying-data covers column graphs alongside histograms, dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots, and mat-types-data only mentions bar charts in passing, so the new point needs its own card.

draft.title: Displaying categorical data
card: Frequency table
lists each category with its frequency, the number of times it occurs. A relative frequency is the frequency as a fraction or percentage of the total.
Bar chart
shows one bar for each category, and the bar's height is its frequency. The bars do not touch, because the categories are separate groups.
Segmented bar chart
splits each bar into parts to compare groups. It is often drawn with percentages, so groups of different sizes can be compared fairly.
Example: a class of 25 students has 10 who walk to school. The relative frequency of walking is 10 ÷ 25 = 0.4, or 40%.
draft.remember: Frequency counts each category. Percentages let groups of different sizes be compared.

a.q: In a survey of 40 students, 14 chose pizza as their favourite lunch. What is the percentage frequency of pizza?
a.why: Percentage frequency = 14 ÷ 40 × 100 = 35%. The number 14 is the frequency, not the percentage, and it only equals a percentage when the total is 100.
a.clue: Divide the frequency by the total, then change to a percentage.

b.q: Class A has 20 students and Class B has 50. In each class, 10 students ride a bike to school. Which statement is correct?
opts: A higher percentage of Class A ride a bike
A higher percentage of Class B ride a bike
The same percentage of each class ride a bike
Class B has a higher frequency of bike riders
b.why: Class A: 10 ÷ 20 = 50%. Class B: 10 ÷ 50 = 20%. The frequencies are equal at 10, which is tempting, but the class sizes differ, so the percentages differ.
b.clue: Work out each class's percentage, not just its count.

b.best: A higher percentage of Class A ride a bike

problems.detail: The question asks for the 'percentage frequency', but the card only names 'relative frequency' (as a fraction or percentage). The term is standard in VCE and easy to infer, but a student reading only the card may hesitate. Consider saying 'percentage frequency' on the card or 'relative frequency, as a percentage' in the question.
